slides.narration: Welcome. Today we study an extract from the autobiography of Nelson Mandela, the first Black President of South Africa. Before anything else, please read the chapter itself in your textbook, First Flight. This lesson does not repeat the text. Instead we will understand it: the events of a historic day, the ideas behind them, Mandela as a person, and how to answer board questions.

slides.narration: Nelson Mandela lived from nineteen eighteen to twenty thirteen. He was a lawyer and a leader of the African National Congress, and he spent about twenty-seven years in prison for fighting apartheid. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize in nineteen ninety-three and became President the next year. Our chapter comes from his autobiography, Long Walk to Freedom, so it is told in the first person.

slides.heading: Background: what apartheid was
slides.body_md: Apartheid was South Africa's system of racial segregation and white minority rule. It became official policy in 1948, but racial domination by law was older, going back to the early twentieth century. The first election open to all races was held in April 1994.

rows: Power held by a white minority
A government elected by all citizens
South Africa isolated by much of the world
Leaders from more than 140 countries attend the inauguration
Army and police enforce the system

visual.alt: Two-column table contrasting South Africa under apartheid, with white minority rule, segregation, isolation, and Mandela in prison, with South Africa from 10 May 1994, with an elected government, equal rights, world leaders attending, generals saluting a Black President, and Mandela as President.
visual.caption: Background, in SOYL's words.

slides.narration: To understand the chapter, you need the background. Apartheid means apartness. It was a system that separated people by race and kept power with a white minority. It became official in nineteen forty-eight, though racial domination by law was older. In April nineteen ninety-four, all South Africans voted for the first time. A few weeks later came the day our chapter describes.

slides.heading: The chapter in six parts
slides.body_md: The first half describes a day; the second half reflects on a life. (A SOYL summary, not the text.)

slides.narration: The chapter has two halves. The first half describes one day: the inauguration, the flypast, the salute and the anthems. The second half reflects on a whole life: the history of injustice and its heroes, courage and human goodness, the two obligations every person has, and how Mandela's idea of freedom grew. Keep these six parts in mind as a map.

slides.heading: Summary 1: the inauguration
slides.body_md: On 10 May 1994, leaders and dignitaries from more than 140 countries gather at the Union Buildings in Pretoria. Mr de Klerk is sworn in as second deputy president, then Thabo Mbeki as first deputy president, and then Mandela as President. In his address, Mandela describes the end of apartheid as a victory shared by everyone and promises a nation of justice and dignity for all.
slides.narration: The chapter opens on the tenth of May, nineteen ninety-four. Guests from more than a hundred and forty countries gather in Pretoria. First Mr de Klerk takes the oath as second deputy president, then Thabo Mbeki as first deputy president, and then Mandela as President. In his speech, Mandela calls the end of apartheid a shared victory and promises justice and dignity for every citizen.

slides.heading: Summary 2: the flypast, the salute and the anthems
slides.body_md: Military aircraft, including jets, helicopters and troop carriers, fly over the Union Buildings: a sign that the armed forces accept the new democratic government. The heads of the defence force and police salute Mandela, though a few years earlier they would have arrested him. Two anthems are sung: white South Africans sing *Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika* and black South Africans sing *Die Stem*.
slides.narration: Next come two powerful symbols. Military aircraft fly overhead, showing that the armed forces now serve a government chosen by everyone. The top generals salute Mandela, though not long ago they would have arrested him. Then two anthems are sung, and each community sings the anthem that used to belong to the other. These moments show reconciliation better than any speech.

slides.heading: Summary 3: looking back at history and its heroes
slides.body_md: Mandela recalls that racial domination was built early in the twentieth century, after the Anglo-Boer War, and lasted for most of it. The day was paid for by thousands who suffered and died, and he grieves that they are absent. Apartheid did lasting harm, but it also produced people of rare courage, such as Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Chief Luthuli, Yusuf Dadoo, Bram Fischer and Robert Sobukwe.
slides.narration: Mandela then looks back. Racial domination began early in the twentieth century, after the Anglo-Boer War, and lasted for most of that century. He insists the victory belongs to the thousands who suffered and died, and he grieves that they cannot share it. Apartheid hurt the nation deeply, yet it also produced remarkable people, like Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu, from whom he learnt about courage.

slides.heading: Check: the order of the ceremony
slides.narration: Your turn. Five events from the inauguration day are shuffled. Put them in the order in which the chapter presents them. Think carefully about who took the oath first.

slides.heading: Summary 4: courage, goodness and two obligations
slides.body_md: From his comrades Mandela learnt that brave people still feel fear; what matters is overcoming it. He believes hatred is learnt, so love can be taught, and even in prison some guards showed him decency. Every person, he says, owes a duty to family and a duty to people and nation. Under apartheid, serving his people cut him off from his family.
slides.narration: The reflections continue. Courage, Mandela learnt, does not mean feeling no fear; it means overcoming it. Hatred is learnt, so love can be taught, and he saw small kindnesses even from prison guards. Then he explains that every person has two duties, to family and to the nation. Apartheid made it impossible to do both, so serving his people cost him his family life.

slides.heading: Summary 5: how his idea of freedom grew
slides.body_md: Mandela's idea of freedom widened at every stage of his life, until it included even those who had oppressed him.

nodes.label: Boy: free within family and custom

visual.alt: Flow of how Mandela's idea of freedom grew: as a boy, free within family and custom; as a student, freedoms for himself; as a young man, the right to work, earn and have a family; then his people's freedom; finally freedom for the oppressor too.
visual.caption: How Mandela's idea of freedom grew (SOYL summary).

slides.narration: Finally, Mandela traces his idea of freedom. As a boy he felt free, as long as he respected his father and his community. As a student he wanted freedoms for himself. As a young man he wanted to work, earn and raise a family. Then he saw that his people were not free, and that became his cause. At the end, he sees that the oppressor must be freed too.

slides.heading: Theme 1: what freedom means
slides.body_md: Freedom in this chapter is not one thing; it grows.
columns:
**Freedom for oneself**

- a boy's carefree life
- a student's personal choices
- an adult's right to work and raise a family

**Freedom for all**

- his people's freedom becomes his cause
- he joins the African National Congress
- even the oppressor must be freed from hatred
slides.narration: The central theme is freedom, and it grows. At first, freedom is personal: a boy's carefree life, a student's choices, an adult's right to a career and family. Then it becomes shared: the freedom of his whole people, which leads him to join the African National Congress. Finally, it includes even the oppressor. In answers, show this growth, not just one stage.

slides.heading: A web of themes

rows: His idea grows from personal freedom to freedom for every South African.
Comrades who felt fear yet kept going.

He credits the thousands who suffered, not himself.

slides.narration: Around freedom sit other themes. Courage, in comrades who were afraid yet kept going. Reconciliation, in the salute and the exchange of anthems. Faith in human goodness, because hatred is learnt. Sacrifice and duty, because his service cost him his family life. And humility, because he credits others for the victory. In long answers, connect two or three themes to show depth.

slides.heading: Check: courage in everyday life
slides.narration: Check yourself. Four students are described. Which one shows courage in exactly Mandela's sense? Remember what he learnt from his comrades.

slides.heading: Theme 2: courage
slides.body_md: Mandela's idea of courage makes bravery possible for ordinary people.
columns:
**Not courage**

- never feeling afraid
- ignoring danger without thinking
- avoiding fear by avoiding the task

**Courage**

- feeling afraid and acting rightly anyway
- choosing duty over comfort
- holding on to hope in hard times
slides.narration: Mandela's idea of courage is worth understanding clearly. Many people think a brave person feels no fear, or rushes into danger without thinking. Mandela disagrees. His comrades were often afraid, yet they kept doing what was right. So bravery lies in what you do while you are afraid. That makes courage a choice open to everyone, including students facing exams or standing up to bullies.

slides.heading: Mandela the man
slides.body_md: Every trait in an answer needs evidence, described in your own words.

rows: He gives the credit for the day to those who suffered and died.
He refuses to hate and sees goodness even in some guards.
He accepts prison and danger to serve his people.
He gives up family life for the struggle.
He sees that the oppressor must be freed too.
He welcomes the exchange of anthems and a government for all.

visual.alt: Table of Mandela's traits with evidence: humble, forgiving, courageous, self-sacrificing, far-sighted, and a unifier.

slides.narration: Let us sketch Mandela as he appears here. He is humble, giving credit to those who suffered. He is forgiving, refusing to hate and seeing goodness even in some guards. He is courageous and self-sacrificing, giving up family life for the struggle. He is far-sighted, seeing that the oppressor must be freed too. And he is a unifier. Back every trait with evidence.

slides.heading: Family or nation?
columns:
**He was right to choose his people**

- apartheid gave him no fair choice
- millions, his own children among them, were unfree
- his sacrifice won freedom for all

**The cost was real**

- his parents, wife and children lost him for decades
- he could not fulfil his duty as a son, husband and father
- the fault lies with the system, not with him
slides.narration: A common exam question asks whether Mandela was right to put his people before his family. One side says yes, because apartheid gave him no fair choice, and his struggle freed millions, including his own children. The other side points to the real cost: his family lost him for decades. The best answers take a clear stand and still acknowledge the other side.

slides.heading: Style and language
bullets: **Autobiography:** first person, so we see events and ideas through Mandela's eyes.
**Reflective tone:** dignified and thoughtful, never bitter or revengeful.
**Contrast:** past and present (prisoner and President; generals who would have arrested him now saluting).
**Metaphor:** freedom described as a long journey, and as something that can be held captive.
**Balanced, speech-like sentences** suited to a statesman.
slides.narration: How does Mandela write? It is an autobiography, so it is in the first person. The tone is reflective and dignified, never bitter. He uses contrast between past and present, such as prisoner and President. He uses metaphors, for example freedom as a long journey, which also gives the book its title. And his balanced sentences sound like a speech, which suits a statesman.

slides.heading: Spotting contrast and metaphor: SOYL's own examples
slides.body_md: A **contrast** sets opposites side by side; a **metaphor** says one thing *is* another. These sentences are SOYL's own, to practise the devices:
bullets: *Yesterday the gate kept us out; today it opens to welcome us.* — contrast
*Her patience was a bridge between the two angry families.* — metaphor
*The boy who once swept the hall now stood on its stage.* — contrast
slides.narration: Here are three sentences of our own to practise. Yesterday the gate kept us out; today it opens to welcome us. That is a contrast between past and present. Her patience was a bridge between two angry families. That is a metaphor. The boy who once swept the hall now stood on its stage. Another contrast. Now find Mandela's own contrasts in your textbook.

slides.narration: These words matter for this chapter. An inauguration is a ceremony that begins a term of office. Dignitaries are people of high rank. Apartheid literally means apartness. Oppression is the cruel use of power. Emancipation means being set free. Deprivation is the lack of basic needs. An obligation is a duty. Reconciliation means making peace after conflict. And a comrade shares your struggle.

slides.heading: Worked example: planning a 6-mark answer
slides.body_md: *Question:* *Mandela was a humble and forgiving leader.* Do you agree?
bullets: **Stand:** agree.
**Points + evidence:** credits those who suffered, not himself; refuses to hate and sees goodness in some guards; wants the oppressor freed too.
**Link:** his humility and forgiveness made reconciliation possible.
**Conclusion:** his greatness lay in generosity, not power.

Give three points with evidence in your own words: he credits those who suffered, he refuses to hate, and he wants the oppressor freed too. Link this to the theme of reconciliation. End with a one-line conclusion. That plan becomes an answer of about one hundred and ten words.

sections.heading: 4. Themes and message
sections.body_md:
- **Freedom:** grows from a personal wish to a shared cause; true freedom includes the oppressor.
- **Courage:** overcoming fear, not lacking it; learnt from comrades.
- **Reconciliation:** the salute of the generals and the exchange of anthems.
- **Faith in human goodness:** hatred is learnt; love comes more easily to people.
- **Sacrifice and duty:** the two obligations; service to the nation cost Mandela his family life.
- **Humility:** the victory belongs to those who suffered.

**Message:** freedom is complete only when it is shared by all, and it is won by courage, sacrifice and the refusal to hate.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Board weight:** reference-to-context extract (5), short answers (3 marks, 40–50 words) and long answers (6 marks, 100–120 words) from *First Flight* (CBSE 2026-27, Section C).

**How marks are awarded:** content (relevant events and ideas, accurately used), interpretation (a clear, supported view), and expression within the word limit.

**Common mistakes**
1. Mixing up the deputies: de Klerk was *second* deputy president, Mbeki *first*.
2. Mixing up the anthems: whites sang *Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika*; blacks sang *Die Stem*.
3. Saying Mandela took the oath first: the deputies were sworn in before him.
4. Describing courage as never feeling fear.
5. Quoting long lines from memory instead of explaining in your own words.

**Remember:** read the chapter in your textbook, *First Flight*.

questions.passage_md: Mandela opens this part of his autobiography by looking outward, at the guests rather than at himself. Leaders and dignitaries from more than 140 countries have travelled to Pretoria, and their presence tells South Africans that the nation once kept at arm's length by the world is now welcomed by it. The ceremony follows a careful order: the two deputy presidents take their oaths first, and only then does Mandela take his. In his address he looks back on the apartheid years as a catastrophe now behind the country and forward to a nation built on justice and dignity for all. A personal triumph is deliberately turned into a shared one.

questions.passage_md: Two moments in the ceremony carry special weight. The first is military. Jets, helicopters and troop carriers pass over the Union Buildings, and the heads of the defence force and police salute the new President and promise to serve him. Mandela reminds the reader that, not many years earlier, these same officers would have arrested him. The display is not a show of force; it is the armed forces accepting a government that every citizen had a vote in choosing. The second moment is musical. Each community sings the anthem that used to belong to the other. The singing may be uncertain, but the gesture says more than any speech could.

questions.passage_md: The ceremony makes most sense when it is placed against the history Mandela recalls. Racial domination in South Africa was older than Mandela himself. It was built by the country's white communities in the early twentieth century, soon after the Anglo-Boer War, and it lasted for most of that century. By the time it was overturned, Mandela was in his seventies. This is why he refuses to treat the day as his own achievement. It was paid for by thousands of men and women who suffered and died, and it saddens him that those who paid the highest price are not there to share it.

questions.passage_md: Mandela makes a surprising claim: the long years of oppression did not only damage South Africa; they also produced its finest people. He names leaders of the struggle such as Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu, Chief Luthuli, Yusuf Dadoo, Bram Fischer and Robert Sobukwe, and treats people of their quality as the country's true strength. From comrades like these he learnt that fear and courage can exist side by side: what makes a person brave is what they do while afraid. questions.passage_md: One of the most hopeful ideas in the extract concerns hatred. Mandela argues that hatred is not inborn: a baby has no opinion about skin colour or faith, so prejudice has to be taught. If it can be learnt, it can be unlearnt, and people can be taught to love instead, which he believes suits human nature better. His evidence comes from his own life. In prison, at the darkest moments, a guard would sometimes show a small act of decency, and that was enough to keep his belief in human goodness alive. For a man who suffered so much under the system, this refusal to hate is remarkable.

questions.passage_md: Mandela describes every person as carrying two kinds of duty: one to the family that raised and depends on them, and one to the wider community and nation. Under a just government, he suggests, nobody would have to choose between the two. In apartheid South Africa, a Black man who tried to serve his people was treated as a criminal and separated from his home. Mandela did not begin by choosing his people over his family; the system forced that choice on him. The result was painful. The more he gave to the struggle, the less he could be present for his parents, his wife or his children.

questions.passage_md: Mandela shows that his idea of freedom grew in stages. As a boy in the countryside he felt entirely free, provided he respected his father and the customs of his community. As a student he wanted freedoms for himself alone, such as choosing how to spend his time. As a young man in Johannesburg he wanted the ordinary rights of an adult: a career, an income and a family life without interference. Only later did he see that his people were no freer than he was, and a private longing grew into a cause. He ends with a striking point: even those who hold power over others are not truly free.

questions.stem_md: Write a character sketch of Nelson Mandela as he appears in this chapter, supporting each quality with evidence. Answer in 100–120 words.

answer.model_answer_md: Mandela emerges as a humble leader. On the greatest day of his life he credits the thousands who suffered and died for freedom, not himself. He is forgiving: he refuses to hate his opponents and believes that even his prison guards had goodness in them. He is courageous in his own definition, mastering fear rather than never feeling it. He is self-sacrificing, accepting separation from his family to serve his people. He is also wise and far-sighted, seeing that the oppressor must be freed along with the oppressed. Finally, he is a unifier, welcoming the anthems of both communities and a government for all. His greatness lies in his generosity of spirit.

questions.stem_md: Trace how Mandela's understanding of freedom changed over his life, as described in the chapter. Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: The stages in order: boyhood → student → young man in Johannesburg → his people's freedom (ANC) → freedom for the oppressor too. Each stage explained in your own words; conclude with his final understanding.

answer.model_answer_md: As a boy, Mandela believed he was completely free, as long as he obeyed his father and the customs of his community. As a student, he wanted personal freedoms, such as deciding how to spend his own time. As a young man in Johannesburg, he wanted the basic rights of an adult: to work, earn a living and raise a family without obstruction. Then he realised that his people were no freer than he was, and his personal longing became a longing for the freedom of all. This is what made him join the African National Congress. Finally, he understood that freedom must be shared by all: the oppressor, ruled by hatred, must be freed as well.

questions.stem_md: Mandela learnt that brave people are not those who feel no fear. How does this idea apply to the life of a student today? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: State Mandela's idea and where it comes from (his comrades) + two or three real student situations (exams, bullying, stage fright) + a conclusion linking back to the chapter.

answer.model_answer_md: Mandela saw that his comrades felt fear like anyone else but refused to let it control them; their courage lay in mastering it. This idea is useful to students. Before a board exam, nervousness is natural, but a brave student prepares steadily instead of avoiding study. A student who sees a classmate being bullied may feel afraid to speak up, yet courage means speaking up anyway. Even standing on stage for a debate takes the same kind of bravery. Fear is not a weakness; giving in to it is. If we accept that courage is a choice, not a gift, then every student can be brave. Mandela's lesson makes courage ordinary and possible for everyone.

questions.stem_md: Mandela says every person has an obligation to family and an obligation to the nation. Was he right to put his people before his family? Give your view in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: A clear stand + the chapter's idea of two obligations + why apartheid made them clash + the cost to his family + a conclusion. A reasoned opposite view (family should come first) can also earn full marks.

answer.model_answer_md: I believe Mandela was right, though the choice was painful. He explains that in a fair society a person can serve both family and nation, but apartheid made that impossible for a Black man. Serving his people meant arrest, punishment and isolation from his home. Had he chosen only his family, millions, including his own children, would have remained unfree. So his sacrifice served his family too, in the long run. Still, the cost was real: his parents, wife and children lost his presence for decades. The fault lies with the unjust system that forced the choice, not with Mandela. His decision shows rare courage and selflessness.

answer.model_answer_md:
10 May 1994, night

I can hardly believe what I saw today in Pretoria. Leaders from all over the world had come for our new President. When Mr de Klerk and Thabo Mbeki were sworn in, and then Nelson Mandela, the crowd went silent and then exploded with joy. Jets and helicopters flew over the Union Buildings, and the generals saluted the man they once hunted. Most moving of all, white people tried to sing our anthem and we sang theirs. My grandfather wept. He said he never thought he would vote, let alone see this. Tonight I feel free, but also responsible. This country belongs to all of us now.

questions.stem_md: How did the inauguration ceremony reflect the change from apartheid to democracy in South Africa? Answer in 100–120 words.
questions.solution_md: Contrast past and present: isolation → world leaders; white minority rule → a President chosen by all; hostile army → loyal generals; division → shared anthems. Conclude with what the ceremony promised.

answer.model_answer_md: The inauguration on 10 May 1994 showed the change in every detail. For decades, a white minority had ruled through apartheid, and South Africa had been isolated. Now leaders from more than 140 countries came to Pretoria to honour a Black President chosen by all citizens. The oaths of a former white President as deputy and of Mandela as President showed a peaceful transfer of power. Jets and troop carriers flew past, and the generals who might once have arrested Mandela saluted him, showing the army's loyalty to democracy. Finally, each community sang the other's anthem. The ceremony turned a long history of division into a public promise of unity and equality.
